newsitem.title: UK: UN food summit next month may fail - UK aid groups.
newsitem.headline: UN food summit next month may fail - UK aid groups.

text.p: A U.N. food summit next month is doomed to fail if it does not ensure food security for those who need it most, a London conference heard on Friday.
The World Food Summit, which will be hosted by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Rome, aims to eradicate rising hunger and malnutrition around the globe.

But speakers at the London conference, held by an alliance of British charities -- the UK Food Group -- said the summit was likely to turn into a mere "talking shop" as its agenda centred around increasing food output rather than making sure supplies reach the hungry.

"Access to safe and adequate food should be recognised as a basic human right and world leaders must endorse this by making it their top priority," said Martin Roberts, coordinator of the UK Food Group.
But one UK farm expert speaking at the London conference said, "I don't think the Summit will achieve anything. Emphasis on production alone and trade liberalisation is very dangerous."
The Summit will aim to halve the number of undernourished by the year 2015, with a mid-term review to ascertain whether that can be achieved by 2010.
Famines that swept through southern Africa in the early 1990s are no longer the cause of human disasters, but some 800 million people are estimated to suffer from lack of food.
Already experts are sceptical whether any fresh cash will be made available to achieve the summit's objective.

Jacques Vercueil, chief of agriculture in the economic development service of the FAO, said donor countries were reluctant to allocate more funds because of evidence that the money was not used fruitfully in the past.
"Who's going to pay for these commitments? Who's going to invest in these rural areas?" asked another speaker.
Finding fresh funds is not the only snag. Experts from poor farming communities said ensuring access to land and water was far more important in curbing hunger.
"I don't think throwing money is the answer," said another British farm expert.

Vandana Shiva, an Indian agricultural researcher, said farmers' emphasis had shifted in recent years to growing cash crops instead of food crops, a move which resulted in unequal distribution of land and food.Silos were bursting at the seams and yet food was scarce for masses of poor and undernourished.

Zimbabwe, for instance, has become one of the world's biggest tobacco growing countries, but many people lack basic food. Its farmers said the Rome summit should consider introducing quotas for cash crops and redistribution of land and water to small holders.
Physical food reserves were needed to be built locally to bridge supply gaps, they said.
